title: Anxious every day for no apparent reason and it’s ruining my life.
body:
After starting therapy, I’ve realised I’ve likely dealt with anxiety for most of my life in different forms.

As a kid, I would get very anxious and even had episodes where I felt like I couldn’t swallow properly at school. That eventually passed. At 11, a major earthquake hit my city and I became very fearful for a long time afterwards - I barely left home and developed rituals like repeated prayers and “touching wood” to stop another one from happening. In my teens, I was extremely self-conscious and also developed an intrusive fear about my dad after seeing something online (I know now this wasn’t real, but it felt very convincing at the time).

Despite all this, I was generally social and fairly happy. I even travelled solo for 3 years starting at 19 and felt confident and independent.

But everything changed around age 24. After COVID, I started having random dizzy spells, and one episode led to fainting. When I started a full-time office job, the symptoms worsened - frequent dizziness, visual disturbances, dissociation, brain fog, floaters, feeling like things weren’t real, and a constant sense of imbalance. I became convinced something physically serious was wrong (like a brain tumour), but scans came back clear.

I was prescribed anxiety medication but stopped after a few days due to side effects (sweating, nausea).

Before an overseas trip last year, I got worse again - neck stiffness, migraines with aura, and I genuinely thought I might have meningitis. I ended up in the ER. But I still went on the trip, and interestingly, most of my symptoms disappeared while I was away. I felt calm and almost “normal” again.

When I came back, I initially thought I was healed. But returning to work triggered everything again — now it’s daily nausea, chest tightness, constant fear, and waves of panic that come out of nowhere. I wake up feeling sick, my neck is constantly tense, and I often feel like I’m on the verge of vomiting or something bad happening. I rarely feel okay anymore. It’s affecting how I do my job and people are starting to pick up on it, which only adds to the stress.

I’m exhausted and scared and just want to feel like myself again. My medication is still sitting there, but I’m afraid of the side effects and the stories I’ve read about it.

Does this sound like anyone else, and is this normal to come out of nowhere at 24 years old? ( I’m now 26) What has helped you? I’m desperate 🥲

title: I disappeared for a few months because my anxiety got really bad
body:
I stopped posting for a while because honestly… my anxiety got pretty bad.

For months, it felt like my brain never shut off. Constant overthinking, stress, random panic, zero mental peace. Even simple things started feeling overwhelming.

I tried all the usual stuff: productivity apps, motivational videos, dopamine detoxes, “fix your life” routines…

Some of it helped a little, but most days I still felt mentally drained.

Over time, I started building small calming habits for myself:

breathing exercises

journaling

staying off my phone more

quiet walks

simple reset routines when my mind got too loud

Nothing life-changing overnight, but little by little it started helping.

I’m still working through it, but I wanted to come back and ask:

What actually helps you calm down when your anxiety gets overwhelming?

I genuinely want to hear what works for other people.

I look at him quickly through my tinted windows and leave. He was bald, tattooed, and burly. He does not follow me as I leave.

I'm completely paranoid now that he somehow did something to my car (tracker, etc). Just had to vent an irrational fear.

title: I'm always anxious no matter how good of a spot I am in
body:
I feel this constant wave of depression wash over me, however I know my life is really good.

I'm 19 and I go to a good college and my internship this summer is lucrative and prestigious ($10k/month), and I'm on track to make $200k+ after college. However the corporate grind burns me out and I feel like a cog in the system. I'm anxious about the future, AI taking my jobs, and I feel apprehension thinking about the next 40 years where I have to sell my soul and play the corporate game, even though it's an incredible privilege.

I have a loving boyfriend, he's very attentive. When we first started dating I was drawn to how supportive he is as a partner about my career, how he helped me recover academically after a major depressive episode. However, as time goes on I he cared less and less about what I do with my time, and at some point just stopped asking and giving advice/support. I know he doesn't owe it to me, however it does break my heart the thing I'm most drawn to him about isn't *there* anymore.

My friends are caring and supportive, they're awesome and always consider my needs. I owe so much to them, however I became so depressed this year I didn't spend much time with them, and I feel relationships start to get icy, and I'm starting to feel out of the loop. I tried hanging out more but there's still a gap and it stresses me out. I also have other friends (not super close) who are too pushy, too selfish, or maybe overall their personality doesn't mesh with mine. I know it's up to me to figure out how to distance myself from them, but the hard feelings and judgement that come with ending friendships give me anxiety.

I have awesome relationships, a great career, I have 10s of thousands saved and can buy anything I want, travel on a whim to anywhere in the world. I'm so grateful for everything...and I shouldn't have complaints but I do. I know if someone else was in my situation they would be super happy. I volunteer at a healing community center where I come into contact with vulnerable people in society (those healing from homelessness, addiction, trauma) and I think how they are less depressed than me with much worse situations.

title: Sometimes I resent my gf for not being able to support and help me through my anxiety
body:
I (25F) have generalized anxiety disorder.

I've had it for about 10 years, been diagnosed for 4. I've been on antidepressants ever since, managed to wean off them for 6 months bc everything had improved tremendously but after 6 months I started having difficulty again and had to start the treatment again. I'm skilled at hiding my anxiety, so I can have a somewhat normal life.

My gf (25F) and I have been together for 3 years. When we met, she said she was an introvert. It became quickly obvious that it wasnt the case. She managed to accept after a year and a half that she had social anxiety and has started a therapy and antidepressants a few months ago.

I do my best to support her and help her progress through her social anxiety and I know she tries to do the same for me. But sometimes, I get incredibly anxious about having to go meet friends, or go to parties, where she is invited but won't go because she's too stressed out, and I feel so hurt. I know if she could she would come and support me. But during those times, I feel so stressed and on my own that I resent her. I understand why she isn't capable of helping, but it doesn't stop me from being disappointed and angry that I have to go through it alone and that I can't rely on her as much as she can. It's not fair of me to feel this way. I just wish I could lay back some time and rest on her.

body: I feel like I don’t see many people talk about this or maybe this is just not very common, but whenever I am surrounded by lots of people, for example during events season like F1 weekend or tourist season or food festival etc where the streets are full of people and cars, I just get super anxious and want to immediately run to an empty space and get out. title: Weed Induced Anxiety
body:
Hello All, posting this on behalf of my fiancé (Female 23). Need advice from people who have went through something similar. 

Background: 

Took a 7.5 THC mg edible about 6 days ago and had a massive anxiety attack. It was my third time taking it and before this experience, it was NEVER bad, I always had a great time. However, this time My resting heart rate didn’t drop below 140 for 3 hours and eventually my friends had to call 911. 

They took me to the hospital and calmed me down with some meds. It was genuinely the scariest anxiety attack I’ve ever experienced, my entire body was in shock, my mouth was the driest it had been and I was shaking uncontrollably. 

When they sent me home, I felt better and could sleep because my heart rate was regulated and when I woke up, I woke up with relief thinking finally it’s gone. However, it’s been a week since then and I get random “ episodes” of anxiety attacks is what it feels like. title: Had to stop working
body:
I am a 36yr old male and over the past couple of years I have witnessed my anxiety take me through horrific drug fueled episodes, which have gotten worse and worse. 

I guess, I am writing this because I am trying to come to terms with my life and what all this means. My anxiety is debillitating and for the longest time I have pushed through it. I have a history of addiction especially with opiates. Recently my addiction feels as though it has hit the heart of my use; my anxiety and depression.

  
My most recent episode saw me overuse kava for 5 days and then due to the kava lose all my motor skills and I couldn't stand up. I ended up falling all over my apartment; I suffered multiple fractures and a lacerated nose. The apartment was damaged and I was in hospital for a week. My anxiety builds (especially at work), then I end up overusing drugs and alcohol and having one of these episodes. After my accident I sat around in my apartment depressed as all hell with my injuries unattended and drank myself into a stupor. 

  
Finally my mum called an ambulance 5 days after my fractures and I was taken to hospital. I moved out of my apartment and have been recovering for a few weeks at my mothers (who is aware of my history and very supportive). Everytime work approached, my anxiety would start ticking again; waking up in a sweat, unable to focus and dry retching. I would then get another week off to recover from my fractures; they hurt but it was more due to my anxiety.

  
I work at a call centre, I find it extremely anxiety provoking. The micro management and the unhappy, unpredictable customers. So I was meant to be going back to work tomorrow. My anxiety was through the roof. debillitating. I had an honest chat with my mother and we both agreed that I would need a prolonged period of time off to get diagnosed properly, medicated and to see a psychologist. 

  
I guess I never realised how serious my anxiety was but when you feel sick from it I feel as though it is worth it to reassess. Nothing is worth the anxiety I feel from it. I also cannot go through another one of my episodes. Luckily I have support around me. I guess what I am saying is, if you feel you're anxiety is stopping you from living a good life. It is okay to be honest about what that means to you.

I will keep everybody updated as I move through this. I know the worst of anxiety and how terrifying it can get. Stay strong everyone and take care of yourselves.

title: Am I wrong for wanting to get the “easier less painful” blood draw to help with my extreme fear of blood tests and needles?
body:
I’ll admit it. I’m an adult and blood draws terrify me. Plain and simple. They just do. I have a phobia of blood and needles, and so the combined experience of a needle being used to plunge blood straight out of my vein into a vile makes me want to throw up and subsequently faint. I am no stranger to blood draws, it’s not like I have never had one. I have had numerous blood tests. I have never actually fainted, but the whole process each time is horrible. It’s mostly mental and anxiety-involved of course. Naturally, every single time, after the whole procedure is over, I usually remark with a woah! That’s it? It’s already done? Wow that was fast, that was over before I even noticed it! But yeah, I mean, I definitely do feel the needle going in, and by all means I feel the negative pressure suction of the blood being sucked out of my vein, flowing bright red as it fills the test tube vile, but yeah, it is never “horribly painful” of course, but it is by all means uncomfortable. Still, the anticipation fills me with pure dread.

And so the time has once again approached me. It’s “that time of the year” again. Time for my annual physical, where after the my doctor sends me to the lab. Just the anticipation of hearing my doctor say that, and the whole process of walking to the lab, waiting in line, sitting in the waiting room for my number to be called, hearing my number being called, sitting in that chair and seeing the arm rest with the needle placed right next to it… That whole scene in my head just sends shivers down my spine. Even the thought of being so anxious I totally just get disoriented and without thinking cut everyone in line on my way to receptionist, only to be called out and told to wait in line like everyone else… Or the phlebotomist sarcastically telling me “ughhh… you’re not gonna faint on me are you… ughhh you’re one of those types…? In my vast experience the worst experience was not necessarily painful, but more of a OH wow. It’s in. Yeah I feel it. Yup. I feel it happening. But mostly it’s just a matter of OK I feel you poking a bit but are you actually going to do it now?? Why are you removing the strap already?? What?? It’s done…??

And so I do what only feels like instinct to me. I avoid the whole process completely. No one is “forcing” me to get a blood test, and so I just avoid it, never even scheduling the physical to begin with. I feel so ashamed of this, as if I am a flawed person. I feel like my life has been put on hold as I just avoid day after day, still too afraid to go through the process. Even scheduling the appointment fills me with anxiety.

I will hear things like “just get it over with!”. And while yeah, the whole process of the blood test would be over before I know it, I just don’t know how I can manage the anticipation anxiety and fear overshadowing getting myself to the lab to begin with. This had me searching for support on how to either make the whole process less stressful or less painful. I discovered a method called the “TAP” (Touch Activated Phlebotomy) system which supposedly “teases” blood out of your arm via the capillaries without an actual needle poke, but it looks like this technology isn’t really something you would find in a typical hospital yet. And then I discovered EMLA cream, which from what I am reading looks like it works wonders with preventing you from actually feeling the blood draw? I want that! Even just the thought of having a cream that would prevent me from feeling the needle and blood suction could be enough to calm my anxiety! I also heard the butterfly needle would be less painful? For me I just shiver thinking about the needle going into my inner elbow, there is something just so… vulnerable about that part of my art, that the thought of a needle in there just makes me want to pass out!

But still, I also feel some shame for this, as if it is “pathetic” that I am so scared about something to trivial, that I should feel ashamed of myself for being such coward when there are “real men fighting real wars out there”. I get it. I already said that I feel ashamed of myself. Even if I do find a way to make my blood test easier, I would still feel shame for “the easy way out” or “not being man enough to get the blood draw like everyone else”, as if I “cheated”, and don’t “deserve” to reward myself for conquering my fear and doing what’s best for my health. But either way, I want to get my blood tested so I can know for certain if I am actually healthy and in good shape. 

Does anyone have any advice for me on perhaps how I can calm myself down or how I could actually make my blood test less traumatic? Thank you very much! And I am really sorry for the long post, I just wanted to see if perhaps anyone else felt this way!

title: Now every time I study, I’m reminded of her
body:
I am 20M from India and she was 20F from Germany. We connected through Reddit because I originally wanted someone to stay consistent with studying. We started doing daily video calls for almost 7 days straight using Pomodoro sessions from like 10:30 am till evening sometimes. During breaks and after sessions we used to talk for hours.

What confuses me is how someone acts so interested and then suddenly disappears like nothing happened.

She used to ask if I ate, if I slept properly, send caring messages, say stuff like “I’m here for you,” talk about her ex, her family problems, her personal life and everything. She barely asked about me but kept sharing things about herself constantly. At one point she even put my city’s climate in her weather application. She also wanted to learn my language (Malayalam) even though she lives in Germany. She told me to learn German while she learns Hindi because Duolingo didn’t have Malayalam or Tamil.

Tell me honestly, how is someone supposed to see all this as “just a friend”?

Then one day she suddenly didn’t show up at all. She was online on WhatsApp but ignored all my messages the whole day. Later she asked “is it my fault?” and I said yeah, a bit, because I literally skipped other plans expecting we would study together like every other day. I mainly wanted someone to help me stay consistent.

After that she slowly disappeared, stopped replying, blocked me on Reddit, and now through another account I saw her posting again trying to find new people to study with.

That’s the part that messed me up. If you don’t want to continue, fine. But why act emotionally close for days, share personal stuff, make someone attached to your daily routine, and then vanish without even explaining?

Now studying itself reminds me of her and it’s become hard to even sit with books properly because those sessions became part of my routine. If she had at least given an explanation, it would have been easier to move on. Ghosting someone without saying anything hurts a lot.

title: Overactivation of the autobiographical memory networks

So, using the autobiographical memory, mental time travel a lot could improve autobiographical memory and episodic( helps with studying). title: Need serious advice
Guysss please help
body:
Lost on career direction at 19, would love some honest input

Hi everyone,

I turned 19 last month, and I am genuinely terrified about my future. I am a general category male from India, and I feel like I am standing at a dead end.

I'll be as detailed and transparent as humanly possible because I don't need generic motivational platitudes or standard "work hard" advice. I need specific, realistic, and executable career blueprints. Every single year I waste pursuing the wrong goal is a year my mother has to live under intense financial pressure.

Here is the exact reality of my life, my limitations, and my aspirations.

The Financial Reality

My dad passed away when my mom was just three months pregnant with me. I am an only child. My mom is 51 years old, works in a low-level state government job, and her entire monthly income is ₹15,000. That is our only active cash flow.

That said, we are not without resources. We own our home, some gold, and ancestral paternal land. Conservatively it adds up to somewhere between ₹90L to ₹1.1Cr. These are real assets that can be sold or used as collateral for a loan if a genuine opportunity demands it. So I do have a financial cushion I can fall back on if needed, just no liquid cash sitting around. I am not looking to gamble recklessly, but I also don't want to rule out paths just because they have an upfront cost.

My extended family consists entirely of state government employees — teachers, principals, government engineers, that sort of background. That is the only ecosystem my mother understands. For her, safety equals a government desk job. I need a path that balances real financial growth with a level of stability she can comprehend.

Some of my cousins are IIM graduates, MBBS doctors, BTech engineers, or settled in Germany. Others are flat-out unemployed. I can see what high-trajectory success looks like but I have no direct mentor to bridge the gap between where I am and where they are.

My Academic Background

10th grade in 2022 — 87%. 12th grade in 2024 — 89.5%, PCB stream.

I appeared for NEET in 2024 and 2025 without success. I am being completely honest with myself: I will not clear the 2026 attempt either. My preparation has hit a hard ceiling and mentally I am completely checked out.

To avoid a blank gap I enrolled in a local BSc program. Major is Zoology, minor Botany, elective Chemistry. My first year CGPA was 6.1 because I was still splitting focus with NEET. I am currently in my 2nd year, exams are coming up in a few months, and I expect to complete my BSc by mid to end of 2027. I am confident I can bring my overall CGPA up to around 7.5 by graduation.

On the side I taught myself high-end video editing and have been freelancing on and off using DaVinci Resolve, CapCut, and AI tools. It is inconsistent money but it proves I can learn complex software, manage clients, and work independently.

Choosing PCB without Math is my biggest regret. It locked me out of engineering routes, data science degrees, and most corporate pipelines. I cannot undo it but I need to know how to work around it.

Paths I Am Considering — I Want Brutal Honesty On Each One

I have been thinking about several different routes and I cannot figure out which one actually makes sense for someone in my situation. Here is every path I have mapped out so far.

Path 1 — BSc then directly go abroad

Is it even possible to get into a decent university in Germany or Europe straight after a BSc in Zoology with a 7.5 CGPA and no Math background? What would I even apply for? Would any university take me seriously or would I get filtered out immediately?

Path 2 — BSc then MSc in India then go to Germany for PhD or work

This feels like the most logical route on paper. Do an MSc in Biotech or a related life sciences field from a decent Indian university, build a stronger academic profile, then apply for a funded PhD in Germany or try to get a research or industry job there. But I want to know if this actually works in practice. Does an MSc from a non-IIT Indian university carry any weight in Germany? Would I get a funded PhD position or would I be competing against people with far stronger profiles? And how long does this whole thing realistically take?

Path 3 — BSc then MBA in India then try to move to Germany or abroad in a corporate role

Some people say doing an MBA first builds the financial foundation and gives you corporate experience that makes moving abroad easier and more stable. Is there any truth to this? Can an MBA from a decent but non-IIM college open doors to multinational companies that eventually allow relocation? Or is this just wishful thinking?

Path 4 — BSc then Ausbildung in Germany

I keep seeing this mentioned everywhere but I still don't fully understand what it is or whether it is relevant for someone with a science background. Is Ausbildung something a BSc graduate should even consider or is it meant for people who have no degree at all? Does it lead to real long term stability and a path to PR or is it a dead end with no upside?

Path 5 — BSc then directly apply for jobs or internships in Germany or other European countries

Is there any realistic way to get hired in Germany or Europe in a life sciences or research-adjacent role straight after a BSc from India? Or is this completely unrealistic without a Master's or PhD?

Path 6 — BSc then pivot to tech through MCA or self-learning and then move abroad

Given that I already have some technical skills from video editing and AI tools, is there a version of this where I transition into a tech-adjacent field, build a portfolio, get a job in India first, and then use that to move abroad? Is this more practical than the research or biotech route given my background?

Path 7 — Stay in India, give government exams, take the safe route

I know this is the one my mother wants. I know it guarantees stability. But I am genuinely asking — is there a version of this path where I don't just stagnate? Is there any government route that offers real growth, decent pay, and doesn't feel like giving up entirely?

The Germany and Abroad Dream — Every Question I Have

Let me be completely honest about what I actually want. I want to earn good money. I want to settle in a country where hard work is actually rewarded, where the quality of life is genuinely different, where I am not grinding forever just to stay afloat. Germany comes to mind first because I have cousins there and I can see the difference with my own eyes. But it doesn't have to be Germany specifically. It could be the Netherlands, Sweden, Canada, Australia, anywhere that gives someone like me a real shot at a good life.

I have been watching YouTube videos, reading Reddit threads, going through blog posts and forums for weeks and I genuinely still have no clear picture of what is possible for someone in my exact situation. Everyone says something different. People say biotech is booming in Europe. Others say you will end up unemployed and broke. Some people swear by Ausbildung as the smartest backdoor into Germany. Others say it is a dead end. I don't know who to believe because most of these people are either uninformed, overly optimistic, or just repeating what they heard from someone else.

I am not here for that. I want to hear from people who have actually done this, who are currently doing this, or who have seriously and realistically planned this out. Not someone who watched the same YouTube videos I did.

Here are every single question I have about going abroad:

Is a BSc in Zoology with a 7.5 CGPA from an Indian university even recognised in Germany? How does the degree recognition process work and how long does it take?

Do I need to learn German or can I realistically survive and build a career in Germany in English? And if German is necessary, how long does it realistically take to get to a working level and how much does it cost to learn?

What is the actual cost of going to Germany for a Master's — tuition, living expenses, visa fees, everything? And how does someone in my financial position fund this without destroying their family?

Are PhD positions in Germany actually paid? I keep hearing they are but I want to know the real numbers — how much do PhD students actually earn in Germany and is it enough to live on without family support?

How does DAAD funding actually work? Who actually gets it? Is it realistic for an Indian student from a non-IIT background or is it mostly for people with exceptional research profiles?

What exams do I need — IELTS, GRE, German language certification? Which ones are actually required and which ones just improve my chances?

What is the realistic timeline from finishing BSc in 2027 to actually landing and settling in Germany? Like a year by year breakdown if possible.

What is the job market actually like in Germany for life sciences graduates — both in research and in industry? Are there actual jobs or do people end up overqualified and underemployed?

What is the path to permanent residency in Germany after studying or working there? How long does it take and how realistic is it for Indians?

Are there other European countries that are easier to get into than Germany but still offer a good quality of life and career prospects in life sciences? Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Finland — any of these worth considering?

What about non-Europe options like Canada or Australia for someone with a life sciences background? Are those more or less accessible than Germany from my current position?

And the most important question of all — given everything I have told you about my background, my profile, my finances, and my timeline, which of these paths actually makes the most sense for me and why? Not what sounds good in theory. What actually works in practice for someone starting from exactly where I am.

The Government Exam Fallback

If I prepare for SSC-CGL, Bank PO, or State PSCs I know I can get stability and my mother would sleep better. But I am deeply afraid of spending my entire 20s grinding for hyper-competitive exams only to end up in a bureaucratic desk job at ₹45k–₹60k a month with no upside and no growth.

What I Am Actually Asking

I finish BSc by mid to end of 2027. I have roughly two years from now to figure out my next move and start working towards it. I cannot afford to waste that time going in the wrong direction.

What should I be doing right now, starting today, to put myself in the best possible position? Which path among everything I have listed is the most realistic given my exact constraints? What does the actual step by step plan look like, and what does the 5 to 10 year outcome look like if I follow it?

Thank you for reading all of this. I just want honest, unfiltered, practical input from people who actually know what they are talking about — not reassurance, not generic advice, and definitely not guesswork.

title: Please read this and help me. I feel completely lost in life right now and I think I’m falling into severe depression.
body:
I chose Arts/Humanities in class 11th not because I loved Arts, but because at that point in my life I had mentally given up on academics completely.

I had no ambition, no direction, no curiosity toward studies, nothing.

My only goal was to somehow survive school, pass 12th with the least effort possible, and get done with it forever.

And in my environment, the “easy” option for students like that was Arts.

I had absolutely no idea what consequences that decision would bring later.

I’m from a region of Rajasthan where most people around me genuinely don’t even know what engineering, research careers, STEM fields, IITs, NITs, IISc, or academic life really are. The entire academic environment is dominated by one thing:

government job exams.

SSC, bank exams, clerical exams, police exams, railway exams — that is what people grow up hearing about. Most students are never exposed to research culture, higher mathematics, computer science, advanced physics, or the broader world of STEM itself.

Science was treated like some distant thing reserved only for “gifted students.”

Even in my school, there was almost no rigorous academic environment, especially in the Arts stream. Our school actually allowed Arts students to take Mathematics, but I didn’t choose it because I had no interest in studying difficult subjects at that time. I only wanted to pass my 11-12th somehow with minimal effort.

So I chose Geography, Political Science, and English Literature instead (Hindi and English were compulsory subjects in Rajasthan Board).

So after class 10th I completely stopped studying Maths and Science. And honestly, within two years I forgot almost everything I had learned in class 10th Maths and Science.

After school, I really only had one realistic option left for my degree:

a B.A. (Bachelor of Arts)

So I took admission in a B.A. program. But honestly, my college itself feels more like a degree-printing shop where I only go for exams and practical submissions.

Then during this period, something unexpected happened.

I randomly started watching Physics videos online.

At first it was simple curiosity.

Then it became an obsession.

For the first time in my life, I encountered ideas that genuinely shook me. Relativity, Quantum Mechanics, Quantum Field Theory, Cosmology, String Theory, M-Theory, Quantum Gravity, QED, philosophy of physics and many other advanced topics — I became deeply obsessed with understanding how reality itself works.

And when I say obsessed, I genuinely mean obsessed.

I studied these topics deeply for hours every day despite having almost no mathematical background to properly understand them formally. I went far deeper into these subjects than most people around me could even imagine. The strange thing is that my forgetting curve is extremely strong, so without revision I forget things very quickly, which I think is just basic human behavior. Even now I’ve forgotten a lot of what I once studied, but at one point I had spent enormous amounts of time trying to understand these ideas.

The ironic part is that I didn’t even remember basic Physics from 10th anymore when all this started.

Still, for the first time in my life, my mind actually felt alive.

For the first time I was studying something I loved.

I was studying because I genuinely loved these subjects.

Nobody around me cared about these subjects. Nobody around me even talked about these subjects. The environment around me was still completely centered around government jobs, and honestly that entire path feels emotionally dead to me.

What made this experience even stranger was that I had never met another Arts student without Mathematics who was interested in Physics or STEM at this level.

I have never met an Arts student who casually knows what Quantum Electrodynamics is.

I have never met an Arts student who talks about Schrödinger or Dirac or Max Planck.

I have never met one who studies advanced Physics topics for fun despite having no formal background.

Sometimes I genuinely wonder if people like that even exist.

If anyone reading this comes from a similar background, please comment your story below because I would genuinely love to meet people like that.

Then reality hit me:

If I truly wanted to study Physics, I needed Mathematics.

At that point it had already been more than 3.5 years since I had studied even class 10th Maths, and I had forgotten almost everything. So I started again from scratch.

Literally from scratch.

Even class 10th Maths took me around 1 month because I rebuilt every concept carefully. Then I started class 11th Maths independently. I completed the first few chapters and even solved some JEE-level problems.

And honestly, I felt proud.

This may sound small to many people here, but where I come from, an Arts student without Maths independently studying class 11th Mathematics seriously is almost unheard of.

But then another reality hit me:

“What exactly am I doing with my life?”

I started feeling that passion alone would not feed me or give me a stable future because my academic background was completely different. So I asked my mother if I could redo my 12th with PCM through NIOS (Open schooling board) and prepare seriously for JEE.

I genuinely wanted a second chance.

I wanted to try for the life I actually wanted instead of the one I accidentally drifted into.

I even dreamed about IISc Bangalore.

But my mother refused.

From the outside it probably looked risky and unrealistic. But even today, Mathematics and Physics do not scare me. Yes, they are difficult for me sometimes, but difficulty is not the problem.

I actually love them.

Meanwhile, during all this confusion, I also taught myself coding from YouTube:

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, MySQL, backend basics — all self-taught.

Then I started worrying about the future of web development because of increasing AI automation trends, so I shifted toward AI/ML. I enrolled in a 45k AI/ML course from a reputed Indian institute (which was too expensive for my lower middle class family). Most students there came from PCM or PCB backgrounds, while I came from Arts.

We studied Python, SQL, Machine Learning models, Deep Learning, ANN, CNN, RNN, LSTM, OOPs, advanced ML concepts and much more.

But here’s the ugly truth:

I procrastinated badly.

Not because I hated the subjects, but because my mind became scattered between too many things at once. Physics, Mathematics, coding, AI/ML, career anxiety, regret about my past decisions, fear about my future — everything started pulling my mind in different directions simultaneously.

I missed classes, delayed practice, accumulated huge backlogs, and slowly reached a point where I started feeling overwhelmed by my own situation. Recently I even failed one of the important tests in the course. If we pass these tests and technical rounds, the institute provides placement assistance and scheduled interviews with companies.

Right now I honestly feel lost.

Part of me wants to complete all my AI/ML backlogs and somehow break into tech despite my Arts background, even though the reality is that almost no companies seriously hire an Arts student who only did an online Data Science/AI-ML course without a proper STEM degree.

Another part of me still wants to restart everything properly, do PCM, prepare seriously for JEE, fight for an IIT or IISc, and pursue Physics, Mathematics, Computer Science, AI/ML or related STEM fields the way I genuinely wanted since I got this realization, even if it takes years.

But I’m already 20 years old.

My parents still want me to prepare for government job exams like almost everyone else around me, but honestly I genuinely cannot imagine myself living that kind of life.

Right now I honestly just need guidance from people who understand these fields better than me.

What should someone like me realistically do from here?

Should I continue trying to build a future through AI/ML despite my weak background and huge backlogs?

Or should I take the risky route, restart with PCM, and seriously pursue the subjects I genuinely love?

I would genuinely appreciate mentorship or advice from anyone experienced enough to guide me honestly.

At my age, many people around me are already starting jobs or building careers, while I feel like I haven’t yet developed any marketable skill or work experience. I also want to start supporting my family as soon as realistically possible, which is making me think more practically now.

SQL

Python

Data Analytics

Data Science basics

Power BI/Tableau

AWS/cloud basics

GitHub/projects/internships

One reason this route attracts me is because even though the IT market is currently down and competitive, it still feels more skill-oriented to me. If I consistently improve myself and build projects, at least I have some level of control over my growth.

At the same time, I also understand that in India, especially for the first job, degrees still matter for shortlisting. Skills matter later too, but many companies still filter candidates based on whether they have a relevant technical degree or not.

Preparing seriously for government exams and accepting the uncertainty/risk.

Doing BCA + aggressively building practical tech skills and trying to become job-ready as early as possible.

Learning technical skills independently while staying at home and maybe doing a distance degree alongside it.

title: I realized I've been “Preparing” for my Life instead of actually living it.
body:
This is kind of uncomfortable to admit, but I think I’ve been using self-improvement as a hiding place.

For years I’ve told myself I’m working on myself. Reading stuff, planning routines, watching videos about discipline, habits, money, health. Always feeling like I’m almost ready. Like once I know a bit more or fix one more thing then I’ll actually start taking my life seriously.

But when I look at my real life not much has really changed.

On paper, things look better. I know more. I can explain what I should be doing pretty well. I’ve got plans and systems and ideas. But the big moves? The uncomfortable ones? The ones that would actually change something? I keep pushing those to later.

I think I finally understand why Preparing feels safe Acting doesn’t.

I think preparing feels safer because you don’t really have to risk anything. You can tell yourself you’re still figuring things out, still learning, still getting ready. It doesn’t feel like failing but it also doesn’t feel like going anywhere.

And honestly my phone plays into this more than I want to admit. A lot of my preparing happens on a screen. Reading another thread, Watching another breakdown, Saving another post. It feels productive but it also keeps me slightly detached from actually doing anything messy in the real world.

What hit me recently was realizing how long I’ve been saying “I’m getting ready.”  
Ready for what? And for how long?

At some point it stops being preparation and starts being delay.

I don’t have a clean lesson here. I’m just starting to notice that my comfort zone isn’t only scrolling or zoning out. It’s also planning, learning, optimizing, and convincing myself I’m being smart by waiting.

I’m trying to move into more action now. Not dramatic stuff. Just smaller, imperfect things that don’t live entirely on my phone or in my head. Things that could actually go wrong.

Still figuring it out Anyone else has noticed this pattern in themselves too ?

**Edit (update) :** Thankyou for all the replies and advices. A few things really stuck with me, especially the idea just do one small Win early in the day.  I also tried planning my day the way someone suggested just blocking small alerts on Google Calendar. I trued Jolt screen time out of curiosity - thought it’d be one of those “meh” productivity apps. Next thing I know, I’m staring at my stats like… 45 HOURS on SCREEN THIS WEEK?? I swear I felt physically ill. It literally Locks my screen when I start scrolling, and that PAUSE message hits harder than any motivational quote ever did. Lowkey changed the way I touch my phone.

title: I almost gave into weed again.

Today marks exactly one month since I quit weed after smoking regularly for about 2 years.

At first it felt harmless, but over time I realized it was slowly turning me into someone isolated, unmotivated socially, and lacking confidence. I’d avoid people, overthink everything, and just kind of exist in my comfort zone instead of actually living. Just trying to make it to the end of the night so i could get my fix.

Since quitting, I’ve felt noticeably better. More energy, sharper thinking, more positivity, and honestly more like myself again. It’s definitely had its ups and downs, but i know staying strong will pay off.

But tonight was the closest I’ve come to giving in. A lot of the cravings hit during lonely or sad moments, and for a minute I almost convinced myself smoking again would help, the lonely and depressing moments i feel can be a lot sometimes and i tend to just make rash decisions sometimes.

Then I remembered something important: weed was never solving the root problem. It was just putting a blanket over it, just coping.

If I want to become more social, more confident, and actually improve my life, I need to be fully present for it, especially during the uncomfortable parts.

I’m really grateful for communities like this because reading other people’s experiences helped pull me out of that mindset tonight. One month down, and I’m proud I reminded myself why I quit in the first place.

Does anyone have any similar experiences?

And how do you guys feel about drinking or even smoking with other people, like at a social event or a hangout? Is that OK for you guys, or is it a “never” type of thing?

title: The real reason leaving your comfort zone doesn’t work
body:
I heard the phrase Leave Your Comfort Zone countless times so I thought that I just wasn’t pushing myself hard enough.

The advice was coupled with:  
Comfort is the biggest killer of dreams  
Life is hard, do the work anyway  
Do what scares you

The core idea I got from this at the time was I just need to work harder. I blamed myself and tried to work even harder and ignore my feelings.

However after burning out several times I finally saw the pattern.

Set a goal ➡️ start working on it ➡️ get excited and impatient ➡️ push beyond capacity ➡️ burnout and forced to slow down

Seeing the cycle was the first step in doing something different. I see cycles as a spinning wheel. Each stage of the cycle reinforces itself and the wheel spins whether we are aware of it or not. 

The key is deceptively simple. Slowing the wheel down requires mindfulness. Slow the body and then the mind slows too. Slow down enough to feel each body part moving. Combine this with journalling and you’re moving from reacting to recording. From things happening to you to things happening for you.

Here’s where I got stuck. I assumed my comfort zone was the place where I was being lazy, avoidant, or too comfortable. 

But looking back, my “comfort zone” was not comfortable at all. It was familiar. It was the familiar loop of pressure, effort, burnout, recovery, and trying again. 

Stillness was what I needed, but stillness felt unsafe. When I slowed down, I had to feel everything I had been pushing past. 

So the real task was not doing more. The real task was to slowly acclimatise to feeling safe enough to rest in stillness.

This changed how I viewed growth. I saw that the cost of not listening to my body was too high. The previous pattern was push too hard and then be forced to slow down to a snails pace. 

The antidote? I call it middle gear ⚙️. It’s not sprinting and it’s not collapse. It’s steady movement with enough awareness to adjust according to your current capacity.

I did it by grounding my body, then 1 step towards my goal.  If I still felt steady, I took one more small step. If not, I grounded again. Rinse and repeat.

So the real reason leaving your comfort zone doesn’t work is because the advice assumes comfort is the problem. But for me, comfort was never the problem. The problem was confusing familiar pressure with growth.  
   
I don’t need to push myself out of comfort. I need to build a steady base I can return to after an honest day’s work.

title: Discipline is fake
body:
The internet is obsessed with telling you motivation is bad, discipline is better, you should be more disciplined and so on. But what kind of discipline are they actually talking about?

What they basically mean is be consistent in doing something, even when you don't want to, forget about your emotions. Maybe I just don't get it, but this concept sounds like full bullshit.

Think about what that actually creates:

Being consistent -> doing the same stuff -> comfort zone????

Being disciplined -> pushing through everything -> burnout?????

I think discipline shouldn't be the goal at all. The real point is small changes and improvements every day.

I also looked up the actual Cambridge definition cuz something felt off:

"training that makes people more willing to obey or more able to control themselves, often in the form of rules, and punishments if these are broken, or the behaviour produced by this training."

Well that's it. Self-control through understanding yourself. The internet's version is blind consistency, which is something completely different.

And the part nobody talks about, people are fckn different. Someone runs on intensity, someone on patience, someone on novelty, someone on rigid rituals. There are literally millions of combinations of what works for who.

The only thing that actually matters is self-reflection. Understanding yourself, your strengths and weaknesses, finding what actually motivates YOU specifically. Then building a routine around that.

General advice doesn't work anymore. Stop trying to be disciplined like someone else, figure out what works for you and build from there.

title: Cost of avoidance and benefits of conflict
body:
There is an issue with what we learn from society. We learn to follow all the rules set before us without questioning them. This can be beneficial when we consider laws regarding danger to others, murder, speeding, robbery etc. However, severe personal issues arise when we learn to not question 'rules' we learn from others. For instance, if you grow up in a passive aggressive household, you learn the ability to show annoyance or frustration in an indirect way. Closing doors loudly, grumbles under your breath, and genuine avoidance of the person causing the distress. This may be the way your household operates, but when you go into the real world, if you still operate in this way you are at a severe disadvantage. You will become frustrated by the lack of being able to express yourself and this feeling will compound into a myriad of issues. Difficulty keeping a partner due to your explosive outbursts or from not letting them into your life. Not being able to speak up when you know you are being treated unfairly at your work, or exploding at the slightest issue at work. All of these and more, because of growing up with parents who didn't know how to model direct and honest communication. Likely because they went through something similar when they were children.

The cost of avoidance here is perpetuating the cycle in your own life. What you stand to gain from conflict, in this case, would be to change something you know into something you understand. You know direct communication is better in every way for your own prosperity and for those around you. It would help you have a conversation about your frustration instead of hiding away your emotions and in the process, releasing what is pent up inside. It would help keep you and your partner on the same page regarding life and allow you to speak your mind at work, with friends or whomever. But making it something you understand requires the challenge of pushing back against what you have learned from your parents. Its not easy, but asking questions helps. Why did they do that? Because this is their first time on earth and they didn't know any better. Does that make it ok? Absolutely not. There is still real world consequences and harm, that has been caused by their actions. How has this harmed you? I can't tell for certain, each person has their own life and their own experiences that color these kinds of 'lessons' they received from their parents. Now the real question, what are you going to do, confront it, or avoid it?

I know if I were a mother these questions would be irrelevant yet people are confused by someone who just does what she wants all day and is never bored, and has zero desire to get a job.

title: I think a large portion of people who fail in self-improvement have a disconnect between concrete action and abstract goals/vision, this can make self-improvement become self-degredation
body:
**TL;DR:** A lot of self-improvement is secretly powered by shame, fantasy and perfectionism. You feel deficient and distort your current self-image into an object of shame, imagine some perfect future version of yourself, get addicted to that vision, make an insane routine based on who you wish you were, keep it up for a week or two, burn out, then feel even worse, causing a cycle that worsens self-image more and more as failures to improve accumulate.

The fix is to stop building your plans around the fantasy version of yourself and redirect the perfectionist tendencies towards something insultingly small and painfully long-term in terms of results. Keep the perfect vision as a vague long-term direction, but reduce it into something almost underwhelmingly small and actually doable. One habit, one reduced version, long enough for it to become consistent, then add the next thing, then the next, over a very long time until consistency is "trained" to make the initial fantasy schedule actually doable and almost automatic, by that point a lot of results will have already come through and the change became real rather than \[motivation -> fantasy -> 1-2 week burst -> burn out -> lose all progress -> repeat\], by trying to be efficient and do everything, you end up with nothing.

For fantasy-prone perfectionists, trying to do everything at once just turns self-improvement into self-harm. Real change is slower, smaller, boring, and less satisfying to the ego than the fantasy.

**The Root/Reason of Self-Improvement & Fantasy**

This post comes from my own experience with my past-self, and a realisation I had over time that helped me finally make a change. I am describing a specific type of person who tries self-improvement, this does not describe everyone of course, some people start self-improvement from a healthy place, so my description is for the people doing it from an unhealthy place.

The idea of self-improvement is usually rooted in a feeling of lack, in a domain or various domains of the self, lack of attention from women, lack of social opportunities or connections, lack of self-confidence or unstable self-image, lack of money or career success, lack of structure generally, lack of muscle mass, lack of healthy weight etc. I know this is obvious, but the feeling of lack is usually comparative, or distorted, or rooted in shame-dynamics.

The person will look at their current self under the lens of distortion, they'll see their set of lacks, and then they'll imagine a version of themselves without these lacks, the perfect body, the magnetism to women, the money and good career, the confident social self etc. They will see their current lacks and amplify their negativity and amplify the negative statement it makes about the self, then compare that distorted self-image with the idealized perfect future self, and this creates motivation to pursue self-improvement as a cure for the damaged negative self-image.

The problem with this is that the fantasy of perfection is something that provides hope, motivation, meaning and encouragement in the moment, and can be intoxicating to ruminate on, and can even bring the illusion of progress just through that preoccupation alone. It is wholly focused on the outcome, the social-proof of the finish line, the perfect self. This makes it a perfect object of fantasy.

**The Cycle of Failure**

But when it comes to making that fantasy into a reality the person usually has to face the opposite side of self-improvement that is faced at the beginning, vague perfect goals that are usually numerous that feel impossible to ground into a real plan in the real world and are set up to create unrealistic routines and improvement attempts that rely on the motivation of obsessing over the fantasy, these eventually burn out and result in failure quite quickly and can feed the negative self-image spiral of being a "failure" or any other negative self-label. The problem is that the actual practical action-oriented side of self-improvement tends to be the opposite of that fantasy in terms of grandiosity or perfection, if we are talking about the kind of actions that actually lead to change. Real efficacious improvement routines are quite boring, small in scale, repetitive, reliant on automating the tedious habit etc.

This effective improvement routine is never produced by the person who relies on the grandiose or motivating perfect vision of the future alone, instead they are produced by taking that perfect vision, and reducing it in scale to what is feasible for the real you in the real world in the real present. Instead of perfection and efficiency towards that perfection being central, boring underwhelming consistency needs to be central, and tolerance of doing less than you truly want deep down.

I used to have this problem badly, and I was not aware of it as I was a teenager back then, thus these endless cycles of \[feel stuck -> form perfection fantasy -> consume self improvement content whilst indulging the fantasy -> make a super unrealistic plan that tries to do everything at once -> succeed for 1-2 weeks -> burn out -> feel even more stuck\] would just repeat and instead of self-improvement or my self image improving, i'd have the opposite, shame and stuckness and i'd be left with self-deterioration, meaning attempting self improvement was actively harming me rather than helping. This comes from there being a major disconnect between the ideal vision of who i wanted to be and what i actually need to do to get there, the egotistical assumption that i'd in an instant, like magic, be able to summon consistency to a large time consuming perfection based schedule, that is what made this all a form of self-harm without me knowing it.

**How I Fixed This Finally**  
When I finally grew a brain and realised what was going on, I was able to instantiate real actionable change by simply changing the way i thought about self-improvement, i'd keep the perfection fantasy as a vague abstract end goal, but instead of basing my schedules upon perfection, i'd make short-medium term imperfect schedules that implement one thing at a time from each category and only do that one thing until it becomes truly consistent, and that one thing would be a much easier and reduced form of the perfect version,

My grandiose fantasy was to be 12% body fat, reach the natural hypertrophy limit for my genetics, maintain a perfect skincare and hair routine, join a band and get a new music-based social group, study pharmacology consistently for an hour a day 5x a week, and to practice guitar for 30 minutes a day where i focus on specific exercises and songs to improve and push my ceiling. Of course this is very unrealistic to do all at once, and trying to force this all at once just feels like bondage to the schedule and you burn out fast without having built the consistency "muscle" first over months to years.

Instead of 4-5 1 hour workouts a week immediately, i'd instead do 2 20 minute workouts a week for a few weeks until it was consistent, then i'd move it up to 3 20 minute workouts for a few more weeks, and slowly build towards this perfect version, and once this single routine feels automatic i'd insert another small reduced form of the fantasy schedule, instead of trying to join a band and find a new social circle through going out 2-3 times a week into unfamiliar bars and local rock concerts, instead i'd go out once a week with friends and simply exist in the area where that music scene exists until i'm used to being there, then maybe i'd go out on my own after a few months and try to talk to people just to get used to it etc.

I realise for people of my constitution and cognition, who are fantasy prone and perfectionists, you have to reroute that perfectionism into something small, very long term, much slower than you'd like, and focused on the most important or valued goal first, for me that was reaching 12% body fat and starting to lift, so i chose a long term slow 500 calorie deficit diet before ever touching a weight, kept that consistent enough, reached the goal, then i added 2 weightlifting sessions of 20 minutes a week whilst starting a lean bulk of a 200-300 calorie surplus, and i'd keep that for weeks, then increase it to 3 times a week for a few weeks, then 4 times, without adding anything else, etc etc.

This has probably been talked about before, but hopefully there's something insightful in this.
